newsitem.title: RUSSIA: IMF team leaves Russia without decision, to return.
newsitem.headline: IMF team leaves Russia without decision, to return.

text.p: An International Monetary Fund mission will leave Moscow on Tuesday without deciding whether Russia should receive the latest tranche of a $10 billion IMF loan, IMF and Russian sources said on Monday.

A senior Russia source participating in the talks said the mission would be back next week after the U.S. Thanksgiving Day holiday and would take a decision then on the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) tranche.
That would allow the IMF board to meet in mid-December and approve disbursal of the $340 million tranche.

"The members of the mission are going back to the U.S. for the holidays and then they will return for a final decision," said the Russian source. "Judging by everything, the decision will be positive for us."
IMF officials confirmed that the mission would return, but said a date has not yet been set.
"It remains to be determined exactly when the mission will be returning to Moscow," Tom Wolf, IMF resident representative in Moscow, told Reuters.
The mission has already left Moscow once without coming to a decision. The main obstacle was Russia's tax shortfall.
The federal government collected only 75 percent of budgeted taxes in the first 10 months of this year, although tax officials expect the figure to close the year at 85 percent.

That is an improvement on August and September, when the dire state of public finances forced the government to get tough, closing tax loopholes and threatening to have the biggest tax debtors declared bankrupt.

The IMF, which sends a mission to Moscow once a month to review economic performance under the three-year EFF credit, delayed a decision on the tranche last month because it wanted to see evidence that tax collection was improving.

But the mission will also want evidence that the last few months' improvement in revenues is not a flash in the pan but a sustainable development. Leaving a decision until next month will give more time for such evidence to accumulate.
Sources close to the talks said taxes, and general structural reform of the Russian economy, were the main issues holding up an agreement.
When the mission left last month, the Russian authorities said that foreign access to the government securities market, and Russian quotas on alcohol imports, were also obstacles.
But the sources said these issues, while still requiring discussion, were not as important as the tax question.
Good relations with the IMF, symbolised by steady payments of tranches under the EFF loan, are an important sign to investors that it is safe to put money into Russia.
But Russia's need for the money itself has become a little less pressing since its $1 billion debut Eurobond, launched last week, was heavily oversubscribed.
